en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Pairs, 28.
The Training Rule on the Hastily Obtained Robe.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain high official, about to go on a journey, sent a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:
"May the venerable ones come; I shall provide them with the rains-retreat gift.
The monks—
Thinking, “The Blessed One has authorized the rains-bathing robe for those who have completed the rains residence,” they did not come out of fear of wrongdoing.
Then that high official complained, grumbled, and became indignant:
“How can it be that the venerable ones will not come when I have sent a messenger?
For I am going with an army;
life is uncertain and death is uncertain.”
The bhikkhus heard that high official grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, having accepted an urgent robe-cloth, to set it aside.
Now at that time, the monks, thinking,
“The Blessed One has allowed us to accept an urgent robe-cloth and set it aside,” [acted accordingly].
Having accepted robes out of haste, they let the robe season pass by.
Those robes remained tied up in bundles on the robe-racks.
While wandering through the lodgings, the Venerable Ānanda saw those robes tied up in bundles on the robe-racks, and seeing them, he said this to the monks:
“Friends, whose robes are these that stand here tied up in bundles in the robe-storage area?
“Friends, they are our ‘urgent’ robes.
“But friends, how long has it been since these robes were set aside?”
Then those monks reported to the Venerable Ānanda exactly what had been said.
The Venerable Ānanda complained, grumbled, and expressed his dissatisfaction:
"How can these monks, having accepted a robe offered as a gift for immediate use, allow the robe season to pass?"
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having rebuked those bhikkhus in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“… ‘Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhus, having accepted an urgent robe-cloth, let the robe-season pass?
‘It is true, Blessed One.’”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How indeed, monks, can those foolish men, having accepted an urgent robe-cloth, let the robe season pass by?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of the unconfident nor for the increase of the confident…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:

“When less than ten days remain until the full moon of the Kattika month of the cold season, if a monk should obtain a robe that is urgently needed, he may accept it, considering it to be urgent; having accepted it, he may keep it until the robe-season.
If he should keep it beyond that time, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.”
"Ten days remaining" means ten days before the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
"The full moon of the month of Kattika."
The invitation ceremony is called Kattika.
An "urgent robe" means:
one who wishes to go to an army, or wishes to go on a journey abroad, or is ill, or is pregnant.
Or faith arises in one who lacks faith, or confidence arises in one who lacks confidence;
if he should send a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus, saying, "May the venerable ones come, I will provide the rainy-season robe," this is called an urgent robe-cloth.
A monk who considers it urgent should accept it; having accepted it, he should store it until the time for robes, making a note of it by saying: “This is an urgent robe.
The time for robes is as follows:
If it should be deposited beyond the last month of the rainy season when the kaṭhina has not been spread,
or beyond five months when the kaṭhina has been spread.
If one lets the last day of the rainy season pass while the kaṭhina has not been spread, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If the kaṭhina has been spread, and one lets the day of the kaṭhina-removal pass, it is an offense involving forfeiture.
It must be forfeited to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And furthermore, monks, it should be relinquished in this way:
…pe… “Venerable sir, this urgent robe-cloth of mine, which has exceeded the robe-season, is to be relinquished.”
"I relinquish this to the Saṅgha" ...
"let him give it" ...
"let them give it" ... [and so forth].
"I give it to the Venerable One.
If, regarding an urgent robe, one perceives it as an urgent robe and lets the robe-season period pass, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If, regarding an urgent robe, one is uncertain and lets the robe-season period pass, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.

If, regarding a robe that is subject to urgency, he perceives it as not subject to urgency and lets the time for making robes pass, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). If, regarding what has not been formally determined, he perceives it as having been determined … [and so on] … if, regarding what has not been assigned, he perceives it as having been assigned … [and so on] … [he lets the time for making robes pass, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession].
Perceiving it as given when it has not been given;
perceiving it as lost when it is not lost;
perceiving it as destroyed when it is not destroyed.
If it has not been burnt, but he perceives it as burnt;
or if it has not been stolen, but he perceives it as stolen, and he lets the robe season pass by, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he uses the forfeited robe without having forfeited it, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not an urgent robe and one perceives it as an urgent robe, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not an urgent robe and one is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not an urgent robe and one perceives it as not an urgent robe, there is no offense.

There is no offense if he resolves [the robe] within the time limit, if he assigns it, if he gives it away, if it is lost, if it is destroyed, if it is burned, if they take it after having stolen it, if they take it on trust, or if he is insane.
"For one who is a first offender":
the eighth training rule concerning a hasty robe is concluded.
